en: The Record of the Meaning of the Huayan Connections:
The Unobstructed Momentum. Section Four: Questions and Answers on the Rhythm of the Text.
First, regarding the "successive inexhaustibility," there are further two gates: first, the gate of multiplicity; second, the gate of categories.
Regarding the origin of the binding:
first, the most pure *dharmadhātu* is unfolded as the two gates of principle and wisdom.
This is precisely what distinguishes bodhi from nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, principle (li) unfolds as essence and function,
while wisdom (zhi) is divided into cause and fruit.
This refers precisely to "Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka" within the title.
Taken as a whole, the preceding and following elements are skillfully combined to form the expression;
this refers precisely to the character "Sūtra" (Jing) within the title.
Nevertheless, encompassing the beginning and the end and capturing its essential pivot,
it is composed of seven characters.
The title is established by summarizing the textual meaning of this entire section.
Furthermore, this title is expanded upon to constitute the First Assembly.
Among these, the first clarifies that the ten oceans and so forth constitute the principle (*tattva*),
which is precisely the "Great Vaipulya" (*Mahāvaipulya*).
The ten wisdoms and so forth constitute knowledge (*jñāna*).
This is precisely the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
which extensively expounds upon the Lotus Treasury World-Ocean and so forth;
it is the fruit accomplished by the ten wisdoms.
This is a brief exposition on the practice of the youth Wei-guang (Vīraprabha) and others;
it is the perfect function arising from the fruit itself.
It provides a general distinction between the causes and fruits of wisdom and principle.
This is how the one assembly is unfolded;
it is the assembly of the fruit of what has been believed.
This single assembly is then unfolded into the seven subsequent assemblies.
Within the preceding causes,
there are distinct divisions such as the practice of vows and so forth, as well as the combined practice and the combined yet distinct practices;
for this reason, they are expanded into seven assemblies.
This refers to the assemblies of the causes for realization.
Since each assembly possesses its own fruit of faith,
there are thus eight assemblies in total, including the preceding ones.
Because the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and so forth all arise in dependence upon objects and do not originate spontaneously;
furthermore, because the practices merge and the causes are fulfilled, one must necessarily realize and enter the *dharmadhātu*.
For these reasons, there is a connection to the subsequent nine assemblies.
Regarding the statement that the separate exposition of the dwelling and so forth, as well as the different stages of practice,
begins with the first discourse and concludes with the sixth discourse.
This comprehensively elucidates the various stages such as "abiding" and so forth;
that is, it clarifies the distinctions between the successive stages through the cultivation of causal practices.
In the seventh and eighth [stages], the two distinct practices are harmonized and subsumed into one without duality.
Samantabhadra’s conduct is unobstructed.
These causal practices must enter the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) to reach ultimate fulfillment;
therefore, this entire sutra extensively elucidates this teaching.
The ascents and descents differ;
in total, there are nine assemblies.
Furthermore, within that which is realized—
It is divided into fifty-five assemblies,
namely those beginning from the Awakening City and ending with the Universal Gate Assembly and so forth;
this is because they testify to and accord with the distinctions in the virtues of the profound dharma-realm of phenomena.
Therefore, including the preceding fundamental assembly,
there are sixty-four assemblies in total.
This [section] uses persons as a locus to clarify the Dharma, thereby manifesting the Distinct Teaching (biejiao).
This is because it relies on persons who differ from those of other teachings.
Furthermore, each and every assembly of knowledge is expanded into an inexhaustible, multilayered assembly,
for all things are fused together without obstruction.
It is like the Rishi taking Sudhana by the hand and causing him to see,
within each and every one of the unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, assemblies of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within those fields.
This is also what follows below:
proceeding toward the Universal Gate Country,
one beholds the assembly of spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) as numerous as the atoms within a trichiliocosm.
These constitute the inexhaustible, infinitely nested assemblies.
Who knows them as they are extensively elucidated in the sutras?
Thus, within the presence of a single spiritual friend...
There are such successive assemblies;
who else could there be?
Furthermore, there are such unspeakably unspeakable, inexhaustible, and successive assemblies.
Pervading all worlds of diverse and similar types, as well as all world-oceans within the paths of atoms and hairs,
the primary and attendant assemblies are layered upon one another, collectively transcending the infinite, successive layers of both origin and conclusion.
Therefore, there are inexhaustible, layered assemblies that fill the ten sessions;
reflect upon this according to the scriptural passages concerning the conclusion and the universal penetration.
As for the second category, which concludes by returning to the source:
Now, examining the context of this passage and various biographical records,
it can be stated briefly that there are five versions.
First, this summarizes the preceding sixty-four assemblies and below, based on the original text;
since the five thousand [verses] and five assemblies and so forth are all subsumed within the ninth assembly,
there are one hundred thousand verses and thirty-nine chapters.
Second, the summary of the preceding infinite, layered assemblies as the middle text:

because each and every one exhausts all worlds of the same and different classes, and exhausts all worlds within the ten directions of the Dharma-realm; and because each and every world-expanse within the atoms of worlds of the same class is filled with tenfold layers of the infinite, and because the principal and attendant [realms] are each filled with tenfold layers of the infinite.
It consists of one thousand four hundred [verses] totaling four hundred and ninety-eight thousand eight hundred gāthās.
Thirdly, it again summarizes the aforementioned "unspeakably unspeakable" and "inexhaustible" successive assemblies to form the Upper Text.

Each and every one [of these] individually exhausts all worlds of similar and dissimilar types, and so on, until all worlds are exhausted; each and every one exhausts all worlds of similar and dissimilar types throughout all ten directions.
Because each [Buddha] exhausts all lands within the atoms of all similar and dissimilar worlds;

because each exhausts all similar and dissimilar worlds, filling them tenfold in layers upon layers, along with all primary and attendant lands and the lands within atoms; because each fills them tenfold in layers upon layers within all similar and dissimilar worlds; and because within the original gate (honmon), all things are filled tenfold in layers upon layers, and within that original gate, they are further measured and filled tenfold.
There are verses numbering as many as the atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms, and chapters numbering as many as the atoms in the four continents.

Furthermore, all things are exhausted; everything is tenfold, layered, and pervasive throughout oceans of worlds; everything is tenfold, layered, and pervasive throughout the entire Dharma-realm; and everything is tenfold, layered, and pervasive throughout the ten directions.
Exhausting all and every [realm], filling ten times ten worlds as numerous as the atoms within them;
exhausting all and every [world], filling ten worlds of both similar and dissimilar types.

Because all things, all things—filling ten times the hair-pore paths of all atoms; all things, all things—the major gates and so forth, filling ten times in their successive layers; and the primary and secondary elements of the fundamental gate and so forth, each filling ten; and because all turnings of all are explained.
This is used as a metaphor for "all turning" and "the turning of all," which refers to the fundamental source.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states:
"Using ink equal in volume to the great ocean and pens gathered like Mount Sumeru."
Even if one were to transcribe the meaning and flavor of each chapter and even each individual sentence of this sutra,
one could not exhaust them.
Furthermore, it says in the sixty-second [fascicle]:
Within each chapter, each gate, each teaching, and each meaning of this Universal Eye Dharma-gate, not even a fraction of these phrases can be grasped,
let alone mastered in their entirety.
As explained extensively in the sutras,
it is impossible to fix the number of verses or the quantity of chapters and sections.
This applies equally to each chapter, each gate, and so forth.
If it is so for the remaining chapters, the remaining gateways, and the primary and attendant factors,
then it is likewise for all gateways and all primary and attendant factors.
If it is so for all chapters, all gateways, and all primary and attendant factors, then it is likewise for all [others].

All else is fully tenfold in every respect; all is fully tenfold in ten successive layers; all is fully tenfold in ten successive gates; and all is thus fully tenfold in ten successive layers of primary and attendant elements.

Since each and every one is fully tenfold, and these tens are layered upon tens; since every chapter and every item is fully tenfold, and every gate is fully tenfold; and since these tens are layered upon tens in terms of the primary and its attendants, and so forth—it is thus.
Each and every phrase and its flavor are tenfold and complete, and the same applies to the primary elements and their associates.
Since each and every phrase, its flavor, the primary elements, and their associates are thus tenfold and complete in a layered manner, so it is.

Since the lands that serve as the basis and so forth are each fully endowed with ten layers of multiplicity, and the principal and attendant elements and so forth are likewise each fully endowed with ten layers of multiplicity,
it is the same for the lands within the atoms of those lands, which are also each fully endowed with ten layers of multiplicity.
This is such that its boundaries cannot be known;
it is not something that can be manifested by words or brush and ink.

This is the very source of the exhaustion and non-exhaustion, the inexhaustible fulfillment of ten times ten throughout the dharma-realm, within every single atom and hair-pore, layer upon layer, fulfilling ten and all things, with each layer of ten fulfilling ten, and so forth.
This is to be understood according to the scriptural text.
This is the original basis for the fifth "Manifestation of the Present.

In this manner, through successive mutual manifestations, they are layered and pervasive, filling the ten [directions] to the point of inexhaustible infinity, equaling the ten [directions] and so forth.
This may be known by consulting the sūtras.
Thus, a sūtra says:
"The events of an eon can still be fully recounted."
It is ineffable and inexhaustible.
Furthermore, it is said:
"If one wishes to expound all dharmas in their entirety..."
Contemplate such statements as "inexhaustible throughout incalculable eons" (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
This is precisely the fundamental principle of the perfect interfusion (*yuánróng*) taught by the ten Buddhas.
However, these ultimate teachings on the exhausted and the inexhaustible flow from the pure dharma-realm;
they are the differentiation within non-differentiation.
Therefore, the Treatise says:
"There is nothing that does not flow from this Dharmakāya," and so forth.
Reflect upon this.
The above has been presented according to a single line of authority;
however, regarding the compilation of the events and the exposition of those events, there exists such a fundamental source.
Furthermore, there are many other lines of authority and many other fundamental sources as well.
Their specific limits are not explicitly revealed;
the number of verses and their categories should be understood by analogy with this.
This is explained in detail as set forth in the sutras.
Regarding the second section, which subsumes those who lack power,
there are further three gateways.
First, the comprehensive is subsumed into the concise;
second, the derivative is traced back to the fundamental;
third, all meanings are fully encompassed.
Regarding the first summary of the extensive [teachings] in brief:
it refers to what is expounded in the collective volumes as the ultimate discourse on the inexhaustible, layered, and fully perfected tenfold [purity].
By means of what has been explained here, it is provisionally demonstrated that the rest—
which is unspeakable and unspeakable— is not something that can be expressed by pen, ink, or other such means.
As the sutra says:
"That which I have expounded is like a single drop of water in the ocean."
Furthermore, it takes as its fundamental basis for metaphorical exposition the teaching of inexhaustible scrolls, infinitely layered and perfectly full,
which are tenfold, circular, and boundlessly interfused; and by means of each individual phrase and sentence, [it reveals this].

Furthermore, they are all bound together in successive layers, filling ten times the inexhaustible and inexhaustible, filling ten times all and everything, and are thus explained as filling ten times.
Moreover, this is the metaphorical explanation of the source.

This is considered the supreme foundation because all the phrases and sentences are interconnected, encompassing all things of the same and different categories, filling ten worlds in successive layers, as well as the principal figures and their retinues filling ten [worlds] in successive layers; thus, everything fills ten [worlds] in successive layers, reaching an inexhaustible and inexhaustible infinity.
Furthermore, the upper fascicle serves as the middle fascicle,
for it encompasses every assembly, every chapter, every passage, and every sentence; moreover,
these all pervade and circulate throughout the entire Dharma-realm and all worlds— down to the paths of atoms and the tips of hairs— and so on, filling ten layers upon ten layers, and so forth.
Because it is universally inclusive;
furthermore, the version from the middle fascicle is taken as the lower version.
Because the universal binding and penetration exhaustively equalizes all assemblies, with each and every one being tenfold in its successive layers.
Furthermore, the lower fascicle constitutes a single assembly;
yet, according to each individual assembly...

Because all are repeatedly fulfilled by ten, all-encompassing and all-pervasive fulfillment by ten is inexhaustible and inexhaustible, and fulfillment by ten is repeatedly fulfilled by ten due to their equality.
As for what is meant by "fulfillment":
In each assembly, ten numbers are taught to signify inexhaustibility.
Furthermore, the entire first assembly as a whole comprises two gates:
that of persons and that of dharmas.
This refers to the aforementioned section on the Dharma;
it is that which later people will realize.
Furthermore, the fascicle constitutes the perfect realization of the mind and its objects.
The assembly of later generations refers to the sequence beginning from the assembly of Mañjuśrī up to the final assembly of Samantabhadra.
Furthermore, these fascicles are divided into seven sections.
This refers to the principle of that which realizes and that which is realized within the title itself;
as previously explained, both cause and effect are fully present therein.
Furthermore, the scroll is composed of three characters;
this is also because it integrates people and so forth by following that Dharma.
Furthermore, the third fascicle consists of two characters;
this is also because they are subsumed and returned to the essence.
The second fascicle consists of [the character] "wei" (為).
This is also because it encompasses and accords with the realization of principle;
thus, while it is a single volume, it is not merely one.
Furthermore, it is because its nature unites all myriad virtues.
Because there is no phenomenon that is not included within inexhaustibility.
Second, regarding the comprehensive inclusion through the meaning:
now, following the flow of the text, I shall speak in terms of its meaning.
"Penetratingly illuminating all assemblies," and so forth,
consists of four characters in total;
these are likewise complete both in their literary form and their meaning.
What are the four?
First is the teaching;
this refers to the fact that although the texts are vast and extensive, [they are nonetheless accessible].
It is subsumed solely within the category of "teaching" (jiao),
specifically the character "sūtra" (jing) in the title;
this has two meanings.
The categories of meaning are immeasurable,
yet they are all subsumed within the single principle of dependent origination;
this is precisely what is meant by "Vaipulya" (Extensive) in the title.
The third part concerns the causes, fruits, virtues, and functions of the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*);
although each of these arises through dependent origination differently.
According to this, it is established that [the title] is comprised solely of the characters "Buddha Avataṃsaka" (佛華嚴),
which are precisely those found in the title.
The four locations:

that is to say, all things, all things, ten times ten, full ten times ten, inexhaustible times inexhaustible, ten times ten of the same and different categories, ten times ten in layers, and the assembly place is but a single location.
The single locus where the characters coincide is precisely this:
the assembly site where all and everything relies upon one another, fully tenfold and layered tenfold.
To speak of it in summary:
Yet the meaning is of a single nature;
the teaching is of a single expression;
and the realization is of a single thought-moment.
The locus is a single atom. Why?
Because one is all.
Because all is one. As the sutra says:
"To know that one is many, and that many is one."
"The meaning and flavor are pure and fully perfected," and so forth;
it further says:
"Within one, understand the immeasurable."
Because within the immeasurable, there is the resolution of them as one and equal.
Master Tong said:
"A single word leaves nothing unsummarized."
This refers to what is called "the extraordinary teaching, which is no different from the ultimate fullness.
Third is "subsuming the branches back into the root."
Now, examining the preceding title:
thus, the single character "Great" (Dà) is the general name for this entire collection;
it refers to the ocean of fruition that is realized.
The two characters "Vaipulya" (fangguǎng) signify the ocean-like qualities of the fruit and its capacity for function;
they comprehensively clarify the causal and operative functions of the entire section.
The single character "Buddha" signifies the wisdom that realizes [this].
The person who thoroughly understands this single teaching is the cause capable of adorning the two characters of "Huayan" (Avataṃsaka).
Through the practice of this entire scripture, one attains perfect resonance with it.
Furthermore, subsuming function into essence refers solely to principle;
subsuming cause into fruit refers solely to the Buddha.
Moreover, it is through the Dharma that one becomes a person.
That persons have no inherent nature is their true nature.
That this nature has no self-nature is its non-nature.
To collectively employ linguistic conventions and combinations of words to express this meaning constitutes the teaching; yet the teaching is itself no teaching.
Why is this? Because the nature of syllables is devoid of intrinsic existence, which is itself liberation;
and because the ocean of fruition transcends words and is inexpressible.
This is precisely the non-differentiation within differentiation.
The Treatise states:
"There is no non-returner who does not realize this Dharma-body."
This is what is meant by that.
Regarding the third point, "unimpeded in both unfolding and rolling up," first the unfolding is explained, followed by the rolling up.
Regarding the first unfolding:
it opens by employing a distinct substance;
thus, substance and function are differentiated.
The distinctions in the nature of conditions and the diversity of dharma-gates are precisely what is meant by "Mahāvaipulya" (Great Vaipulya).
Because causes and effects differ,
their practices and understandings are distinct,
and there are differences in their cultivation and realization.
There is a distinction between master and disciple;
this refers precisely to the Buddha’s *Avataṃsaka*.
It is precisely because there is a distinction in how the sutra is woven together and its meaning is elucidated.
This refers to the teaching that all things are inexhaustible, inexhaustibly fulfilling ten layers, and those ten layers further fulfilling ten;
it is precisely these characters of the sutra.
This is explained in detail elsewhere.
Understand it thus.
As for the two volumes,
there are further five gates.
First, the positions are subsumed through unification;
second, the assemblies are gathered by way of the persons;
third, the Dharma is elucidated by means of the persons.
Fourth, the perfect interfusion of objects and wisdom;
fifth, the submergence of the ocean of cause and effect.
Regarding the first:
However, this scriptural passage contains omissions and inversions;
it consists of three sections in total,
none of which fail to be briefly summarized.
This refers to understanding, practice, and realization.
Within the stage of understanding,
there are naturally two objects.
That is, within the first assembly,
he cites the fruits of the Buddha’s environment and his person (the *āśraya* and *āśrita*) and so forth,
exhorting [beings] to give rise to faith and delight.
According to this text,
it is titled "The Section on Exhorting Joyful Faith by Pointing to the Fruit.
Second, the explanation.
From the second assembly through to the end of the sixth assembly,
it extensively explains therein the characteristics of the sequential arising of understanding within the four stages, beginning with "abiding" (*sthiti*).
According to this text:
This is titled "The Section on Cultivating the Cause to Accord with the Fruit and Giving Rise to Understanding.
This section also has two parts.
The first is "Practice According to the Stages."
Second, the practice of different stages.
In the first [section], within the seventh assembly,
the preceding assembly is separately explained to establish the basis of the stages.
The practices of Samantabhadra are universally integrated into a single reality;
because they are the practices of Samantabhadra,
there are thus two successive assemblies.
Therefore, the reason why the *Samantaprabhāsa* Dharma-assembly is said to have two successive gatherings is intended to mean this very point.
Thus, it is according to this text.
This is called the section on "Entrusting the Dharma to Advance and Accomplish Practice.
How is this known?
It is because the matter occurs within the Second Assembly at Universal Radiance.
If it were not so, why would there not be a third assembly and so forth?
For the second assembly was the beginning of the exposition of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*.
Now that the *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Commentary) and other works have been completed,
it is logically appropriate to begin from the beginning;
therefore, I shall once again assemble the practices of Samantabhadra.
The reason for not doing so here is also to reveal that throughout all the assemblies, during the second seven-day period,
the teaching was expounded instantaneously and universally without any sequence of before or after. Why is this?
Whether spoken individually or repeated, both are identical to the second seven-day period;
thus there are three proofs.
In the ninth assembly:
Furthermore, regarding the fruits previously mentioned as the gateway for entering realization according to the five stages of persons:
since one initially aspires to and delights in the preceding fruit,
one thereby gives rise to faith and understanding.
Having already integrated understanding and accomplished practice,
one immediately realizes the aforementioned fruit;
therefore, this constitutes the subsequent integration.
Is this a separate proof of the treatise?
According to the text, it is simply the preceding assembly.
If it were not so, [the following would apply].
Raising the previous point: when that fruit gives rise to faith and understanding,
and once that understanding has been integrated into practice,
does one then separately realize that previous fruit?
Now, based on the sequence of the textual meanings,
it is known that "the first assembly" refers to the very first assembly. Therefore,
[the text] is divided into three sections in total.
This is in complete accord with the scriptural text;
it can be understood through careful reflection.
Second, regarding the classification and synthesis according to persons:
Furthermore, these are all merged into a single assembly,
which is exclusively the ninth assembly. Why is this so?
The first assembly is the foundational stage for the preceding interpretations and so forth;
when the subsequent interpretation reaches fulfillment, it integrates with the preceding differentiated interpretations to form a single,
perfectly harmonious practice and virtue.
Having realized and entered the aforementioned dharmas,
one ultimately transcends all words;
therefore, the ninth stage relies upon a person to clarify the realization of the Dharma-realm.
To manifest this profound meaning,
the ninth assembly clarifies entering realization by relying upon a person.
Regarding the phrase "entrusting to those who understand," this refers to the ninth assembly,
wherein the Tathāgata himself entered the Lion’s Vigorous Display Samādhi.
This causes all bodhisattvas to realize and enter the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
This is the exhortation to rejoice in the previously mentioned fruit;
it corresponds to the first assembly.
This is because the Tathāgata himself entered the *vega-prāpta* (Fenxun) samādhi, desiring to cause all bodhisattvas to likewise realize and enter it.
Furthermore, from Mañjuśrī at the beginning to Gopikā at the end,
these represent the signs of generating understanding through the convergence of prior cultivation of causes with the realization of the fruit.
This refers precisely to the first seven assemblies.
It is because Sudhana inquires of various people in order to seek distinct faiths and understandings, and to achieve extensive and universal knowledge.
Later, Māyā and Maitreya arrive;
these two previously entrusted themselves to the Dharma, advanced in their practice, and achieved non-duality.
This shall take place at the seventh assembly.
In the eighth assembly, both [Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī] clarify the ultimate, unimpeded, perfectly interfused, and sovereign nature of Samantabhadra’s great conduct;
whereas Mañjuśrī, relying upon his *ratnāvalī* (necklace),
clarifies that he is fully endowed with the ten thousand virtues of the two adornments of merit and wisdom.
Furthermore, Māyā is the mother of all Buddhas;
because she represents the fulfillment of practice that can give birth to a Buddha,
Samantabhadra is placed at the end.
When one takes the dharma-realm of dependent origination as the object of focus,
one manifests the completion of practice and thereby attains entry into realization.
Therefore, this corresponds to the ninth assembly;
it constitutes the section on entering realization through reliance upon others,
as one beholds as many spiritual friends and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva as there are atoms in a dust mote.
Furthermore, because there is no further postponement.
Regarding the third [category], those who include people according to their status:
this refers to those within a circle of learned associates.
Furthermore, from Mañjuśrī at the beginning to Gopikā at the end,
there are forty-one individuals in total;
these are termed the "characteristics of practice through the stages of entrustment."
That is to say, one relies on the four dharmas,
such as "entrusting" and so forth, to seek understanding through others and practices them progressively.
The second [section], beginning from Māyā and ending with the youth Śrīsaṃbhava and others,
comprises eleven persons in total;
this is called "Entering the True Reality by Means of the Convergence of Conditions."
By immediately uniting the former abidings and so forth,
one accomplishes both the universal and particular practices,
thereby harmonizing with the Dharma-realm.
The third, the single personage Maitreya, is named "The Cause for Gathering Virtuous Qualities" (攝德成因相).
This refers to the preceding universal gate based on the stages (*āśraya-sthāna*),
which serves collectively as the cause for entering into realization.
In the fourth stage, the single figure of Mañjuśrī represents wisdom illuminating the non-dual aspect; that is,
the ultimate integration and lucid awakening held within one's being,
which illuminates the preceding practices and so forth.
The single, truly perfect wisdom has no further distinctions such as prior or subsequent, clarity or obscurity.
The fifth, the single name "Samantabhadra," signifies the vast characteristic of manifesting the cause.
Thus, initial awakening is identical to the fundamental;
great wisdom manifests before one, pervading and encompassing the entire Dharma-realm,
reaching everywhere without exception.
It is universally inclusive.
Regarding the fourth point, the perfect interfusion of object and wisdom,
we again refer to the aforementioned persons.
In summary, there are two:
first, Mañjuśrī,
who is the wisdom that realizes [the truth].
The former refers to the stages of practice and so forth;
the second is Samantabhadra,
which is the dharma-realm that is realized.
This is precisely that which is to be believed and entered.
Why? Because Mañjuśrī corresponds to the stage of Prajñāpāramitā.
Samantabhadra is the gateway to the Dharma-realm.
As for how this is known,
the Master said:
Regarding the "Three Pitakas," there is a sutra that speaks in this manner;
furthermore, if one examines the meaning, intent, and literary flow within this sutra:
There is indeed profound truth in this.
Furthermore, since the ancient masters have already determined that the later Mañjuśrī is named for the non-dual nature of wisdom and illumination,
we know that all the individuals mentioned previously are in fact none other than this single later Mañjuśrī.
Therefore, the subsequent text states:
"Sudhana returned, passing through one hundred and ten cities,
and once again met with Mañjuśrī."
This is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī instructed me in the methods of counting strokes and so forth.
Moreover, the subsequent passage states:
"By the power of Mañjuśrī’s recollection," and so forth.
Furthermore, the subsequent passage states:
"Good son, Mañjuśrī is your spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra)."
It can cause you to be born into the family of the Tathāgata,
nurture your roots of goodness, and accumulate a mass of merit until your great vows are fulfilled.
Regarding the phrase "The purification of all dharma-gates is entirely due to the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī":
since one has already fully perfected the realization of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), [the purification occurs].
Each cause is fulfilled because Samantabhadra abides at the rear;
as the subsequent text states:
"I manifest the realm of the Buddha within each and every pore.
Thus he observes with clarity, and so forth.
It further says:
"You should fully contemplate my pure Dharma-body, etc.
The commentary explains:
Since he has been instructed to contemplate the pure Dharma-body, [the subsequent text follows].
Thus we know that Sudhana’s vision of Samantabhadra is precisely the realization of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Furthermore, these may be condensed into one.
This means that object and wisdom are of one suchness, without any distinction.
Therefore, in the subsequent passage, Mañjuśrī no longer has the perception of a body.
Why is the teaching thus?
Because one first sees Mañjuśrī,
it clarifies that Sudhana’s faith begins with him;
until the end, when he no longer sees [Mañjuśrī], one sees the scripture on Sudhana’s fulfillment of wisdom.
The various individuals in between are all stages in Sudhana’s sequence of practice;
as Sudhana has exhausted his obstacles and eliminated his delusions,
he does not necessarily stir a thought.
Therefore, reflecting back, there is only the original mind and nothing else;
this is the meaning of "not seeing anything afterwards."
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Arisen from the wisdom of Mañjuśrī," and so forth;
this also signifies that within the treatise, initial enlightenment (ādi-bodhi) is identical with fundamental enlightenment (mūla-bodhi).
This refers to the absence of any distinction between non-enlightenment and enlightenment.
Fifth, "merging equally into the ocean of fruition" means:
This means that because the causal practice is perfected, one passes away into the ocean of fruition;
it is luminous from beginning to end, a perfect fusion of all virtues,
beyond words and transcending thought, realized only through direct correspondence with the truth.
Thus, these are spoken of as gateways for the sake of exposition;
in reality, the mind has no before or after.
Therefore, its rolling up and unfolding is such that it cannot be easily described as being subject to obstruction.
Regarding "taking," reflect upon it according to the text.
Therefore, the subsequent passage says:
"In this way, the true son of the Buddha..."
When sentient beings desire to deliberate upon this most profound and subtle meaning,
their minds become confused and they fall into madness.
This is what is meant by that.
Regarding the fourth question-and-answer session, which follows the momentum of the text, there are also two parts.
The first is the question-and-answer session that synthesizes the preceding material.
Second, the exhortation to practice and study.
Regarding the first section on questions and answers concerning the preceding assembly:
since it was previously stated that this is the Māyā Assembly, [the question is asked].
If the preceding conditions constitute a single reality, how can it be that after the assembly, there are ten people who differ?
Answer: It is because after the assembly, there are ten people.
This demonstrates that dependent origination is inexhaustible;
it is manifested by means of ten aspects. What are they?
Because they do not depart from Māyā,
they are all the actual virtues of Māyā;
this refers to the shared cultivation throughout the five preceding periods of three ages.
As for the ultimate birth of the Buddhas,
a sutra states:
"I am the mother of all Buddhas."
The statement that "all Buddhas are born from me" and so forth can also signify that all stages are mutually fused and integrated, expanding and contracting without obstruction. Therefore,
each and every stage is itself the realization of Buddhahood.
This is what is intended here.
Question: Since Māyā has no intrinsic substance, how do all the stages come together to be established?
It is the same for all other people as well.
Why do they not all possess these ten?
Answer: It is because within Māyā, these ten persons were fully present.
This is precisely what each of the aforementioned individuals possesses.
Why is this? Because Māyā is the very embodiment of all those people mentioned previously.
This is because they are taken as a single body;
for each and every person is Māyā, and Māyā is each and every person.
The intention behind stating that Māyā alone contained ten people within her womb is as follows.
Question: Is Māyā not the same as the aforementioned individuals?
If it is said that "this one possesses [the marks] and others also possess them," then might these people not simply be the later Māyā?
Why is it that she possessed them earlier but does not possess them later?
Answer: Māyā is the general [category], while the others are the specific ones;
together they cause the general to possess the specific.
Why is this? Because if the individual [aspects] are not ultimate,
the collective [whole] is likewise not ultimate.
Since wisdom has not yet reached its ultimate consummation,
there is nothing further to be distinguished;
how, then, could it be complete?
Therefore, that which is fully present within Māyā is also fully present in other persons.
Question: Within the eight assemblies—

For what reason do the four assemblies of the *Ascension to Heaven* (Śakraprasenajit-sūtra) all state that [the Buddha] "ascended to heaven without rising from the Bodhi tree," whereas the three assemblies among humans do not say he "ascended there without leaving this place"?
The answer to this has two meanings:
first, based on understanding;
second, in terms of practice.
Within the initial explanation, there are again three parts:
first, the proximate; second, the remote; and third, the general.
First, regarding the proximate:
Because the human realm and the [heavenly] ground are adjacent and not far apart,
it is a natural principle (dharmatā) that they are included [in this category] without needing to be explicitly stated.
This is why it is not said that one rises to that [realm] without first departing from this one.
As for "the distant," because the bodies of the human and celestial classes are extremely remote and dissimilar, they do not mutually encompass one another and are difficult to comprehend; therefore,
the subsequent section is introduced by means of the preceding one.
This reveals that dependent origination is unimpeded and mutually interfused.
Third, regarding "the general":
this means subsuming the particular within the general.
Though they differ in their ascent and descent within the totality,
all maintain that one ascends to that realm without departing from the tree of awakening.
This further clarifies that the universal gate itself possesses distinct characteristics:
although it departs from within that [particular],
it constantly remains here.
This is done because one wishes to produce understanding in sentient beings;
thus, by citing the latter, the former is implied.
Second, regarding the practitioner, there are again two [aspects].
First, the presentation of the meaning;
second, the resolution of objections.
Regarding the first:
However, assemblies such as those for ascending to heaven are discussed based on their specific interpretations and locations;
since there is no distinction in the practice once the interpretation is complete,
the latter two are not discussed.
Those who do not resemble the heavens possess this intention.
Second, they rectify their own station through faith.
Therefore, it is not mentioned in those two places.
Question: Above, it was stated that Sudhana did not see Mañjuśrī;
this immediately indicates that his wisdom was perfected.
If it is the case that only this initial mind is without difference, why does the sūtra speak of Sudhana traversing various stages?
The answer is: there are two kinds of "traversing various stages" spoken of in the sūtra.
First, regarding the teaching and practice, it is said that the teachings possess successive stages and levels of distinction;
Sudhana’s progression through these stages is explained based on this principle.

Second, regarding the perfect integration of meaning: because the great *dharmadhātu* of dependent origination is simultaneously complete and lacks distinctions such as sequence, position, or priority and posteriority, Sudhana’s single lifetime is explained in accordance with this principle.
Now, I shall cause [the reader] to discern this through two meanings.
Nevertheless, the progression through the stages does not depart from the initial resolve;
that one lifetime has not yet begun, yet much has been cultivated over many kalpas, is precisely what is intended by this.
Therefore, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"A single thought-moment is immeasurable eons;
immeasurable eons are a single thought-moment," and so forth.
Now, speaking in terms of doctrine and meaning,
this is termed the "One Vehicle of Shared Teaching. If, however,
one speaks in terms of doctrine subsumed by meaning, [it is the One Vehicle of Distinct Teaching].
This is precisely what is called the distinct teaching (biejiao) of the One Vehicle.
However, the fact that Sudhana traveled through various stages without ever departing from his initial resolve is based on this very teaching.
Question: Why is it that at the very end there is no further instruction regarding the future, nor any concluding summary and so forth?
Answer: Because the meeting with Mañjuśrī signifies that Sudhana’s causal practice has already reached its ultimate completion.
Later, when Samantabhadra Bodhisattva explains that Sudhana has attained realization in accordance with the teaching,
it is because upon seeing him once, both his mind and his practice were simultaneously perfected.
Therefore, [the text] further points out that there is nothing subsequent to this.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states:
"Within the interlacing nodes of the marks and signs of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, and within each of his pores,
Sudhana beheld unspeakably unspeakable oceans of worlds filled with Buddhas."
The second refers to Tathāgatas, numbering unspeakably unspeakable,
with great Bodhisattvas as their retinue, and so forth;
this is as previously explained.
The second section is the exhortation for practitioners to cultivate [the path].
What has been stated above in the introduction to the sutra is as brief as looking at the heavens through a tube.
The remaining momentum is manifold;
its limits are unknown,
even if one were to exhaustively investigate throughout all future kalpas.
I vow to complete this practice.
May I always maintain this thought throughout the succession of abandoning one body and receiving another.
If there are those who have faith and take refuge to cultivate and study, may they likewise do so.
One will swiftly realize Bodhi.
Therefore, seeing and hearing [the Dharma] necessarily establishes a firm seed;
one should further give rise to great joy, rejoicing in oneself and longing for such a rare encounter.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Sudhana, you should give rise to great joy,
for before long you shall attain the great fruit of retribution."
While immeasurable bodhisattvas have practiced for immeasurable eons,
you now possess all these virtues in a single lifetime;
this applies even to those who wish to attain such a Dharma.
It is said that this concentration is as practiced by Sudhana and others;
furthermore,
it is stated that the Buddhas of the past exclusively sought awakening by cultivating this practice.
Throughout immeasurable kalpas amidst all conditioned phenomena, one has experienced immeasurable suffering, yet still has not encountered [it]. ...
up to the point where it says:
They shall obtain great and wholesome benefits,
fulfill their great vows,
and draw near to all Buddhas.
"Being a true son of the Buddha,
one will certainly attain the Way of Buddhahood," and so forth,
as explained in detail in the sutras.
In accordance with this,
a manuscript of one fascicle titled *Kegon-kammaku-giki* (Record of the Meaning of the Vital Lineage of the Avataṃsaka) states:
"The fifth day of the third month of the late spring in the fifth year of Eiren, the Dingyou year."
